summary: Describes the User-based Security Model for SNMPv3, which provides message-level security such as authentication and privacy for management traffic. It includes a MIB for managing its configuration. It obsoletes RFC 2274 and was replaced by RFC 3414.

eli5.summary: This adds user names, passwords and secret scrambling to network-monitoring messages, so strangers can't read or fake them.

questions: how does snmpv3 prevent replay attacks
subtitle: Per-user authentication, encryption and replay protection for SNMPv3 management messages.

tldr.problem: Network management messages can be altered, forged or replayed in transit, and an SNMP agent needs to know which user really sent a request.
tldr.mechanism: Each message carries a user name, engine identifier and time indicators. HMAC-MD5-96 or HMAC-SHA-96 authenticates the whole message, CBC-DES can hide the payload, and per-engine localized keys and a 150-second time window limit replay.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2574 obsoleted RFC 2274 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 3414.

today: RFC 2574 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 2274, and it has since been obsoleted by RFC 3414, which now defines the User-based Security Model.

sections.title: Threats and Goals
sections.content:
The User-based Security Model (USM) is the security model for SNMP version 3. It is built around the traditional idea of a user, identified by a userName, with whom security information is associated. It provides message-level security for the SNMP architecture of RFC 2571 and includes a MIB for managing its own configuration.

The principal threats it must stop are modification of information (altering a message in transit) and masquerade (acting as another user). It gives only limited protection against disclosure (eavesdropping) and message stream modification (malicious reordering, delay or replay). It does not try to stop denial of service or traffic analysis.

Its goals are to verify that a message was not modified, to verify the identity of the user behind it, to detect messages that were not generated recently, and to protect content from disclosure when needed. Where effective management in times of network stress conflicts with security, the design prefers management. It also must not depend on other services such as NTP or key management protocols.
sections.eli5: Imagine the notes a building manager sends to the boiler. This makes sure nobody changed a note, nobody pretended to be the manager, and nobody re-sent an old note.

sections.title: Users, Keys and Authoritative Engines
sections.content:
An SNMP engine must know every user it serves. A user has a userName, a securityName, an authProtocol with an authKey, and a privProtocol with a privKey. The keys are never readable through SNMP, and can be changed remotely only through the dedicated key change objects.

For each exchange one engine is authoritative. If the message expects a response, the receiver is authoritative. If it does not, the sender is. The authoritative engine's identifier and clock are used to check timeliness.

To avoid one password working everywhere, USM uses key localization. The user's password becomes a key, then the authoritative engine's snmpEngineID is wrapped between two copies of that key and hashed with MD5 or SHA. This gives a different secret for each engine, even though the user remembers one password.
sections.eli5: You remember one password, but each device you manage gets its own secret made by mixing your password with that device's name. If one device leaks, the others stay safe.

sections.title: Replay Protection, Time Windows and Discovery
sections.content:
Each engine keeps snmpEngineID, snmpEngineBoots (reboots since the ID was configured) and snmpEngineTime (seconds since the last boot count change). Boots must be kept in non-volatile storage, so no battery-backed clock is needed. Each authenticated message carries the authoritative engine's ID, boots and time. The receiver checks that they are within a Time Window of 150 seconds. The timeliness check is only done when authentication is applied. If boots ever reaches 2147483647 it latches and messages fail with notInTimeWindow until an engine is manually reconfigured.

A non-authoritative engine keeps its own copy of the authoritative engine's values, including latestReceivedEngineTime, and updates them as authentic messages arrive. No separate synchronization step is needed.

Discovery lets an engine learn the remote ID. It sends a Request with noAuthNoPriv, a zero-length user name and engine ID, and an empty variable binding list. The reply is a Report carrying the ID and a usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs counter. For authenticated traffic it then sends an authenticated Request with boots and time set to zero, and the Report with usmStatsNotInTimeWindows supplies current values.
sections.eli5: Each device keeps a count of how many times it has restarted and a stopwatch. Messages carry both, so an old message is spotted as too old and thrown away.

sections.title: The Security Parameters Field
sections.content:
USM puts its data in the SNMPv3 msgSecurityParameters field, an OCTET STRING holding a BER-encoded sequence of six values.

  • msgAuthoritativeEngineID: the authoritative engine's identifier.
  • msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots and msgAuthoritativeEngineTime: its boots and time, each from 0 to 2147483647.
  • msgUserName: the user the message is for, up to 32 octets. A zero-length name matches no user but can be used for discovery.
  • msgAuthenticationParameters: set by the authentication protocol, such as the message authentication code.
  • msgPrivacyParameters: set by the privacy protocol, such as the DES salt.
sections.eli5: It is the label on the envelope: who is the sender acting for, which device, what time its clock says, plus a seal and a scrambling note.

sections.title: Authentication and Privacy Protocols
sections.content:
The authentication and privacy protocols are described in separate sections so they can be replaced or supplemented later. If authentication is used, the complete message is checked.

HMAC-MD5-96 is the first authentication protocol that MUST be supported. A 128-bit MD5 digest is computed in HMAC mode over the message, and the first 96 bits (12 octets) are carried in the message. Its authentication key is 16 octets. HMAC-SHA-96 SHOULD be supported. It uses a 160-bit SHA digest, again truncated to 12 octets, with a 20-octet key.

CBC-DES is the privacy protocol. The scopedPDU is encrypted, padded to a multiple of 8 octets, in Cipher Block Chaining mode. The first 8 octets of the 16-octet privacy key are the DES key. The last 8 octets are XORed with a per-packet salt to form the initialization vector, and the salt travels in msgPrivacyParameters. A message using privacy MUST also be authenticated. Implementing a privacy protocol is optional.
sections.eli5: Authentication is a tamper-proof seal on the envelope. Privacy is writing the note in a secret code first. You need the seal even when you use the code.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An authenticated message stays valid for about 150 seconds and can be replayed in that period. So engines must discard Responses with no outstanding Request, and use different msgID and request-id values for all Requests in a Time Window. A command generator sending state-altering messages should wait for an acknowledgement, or for the previous message to expire. The snmpSetSerialNo object can also order Set operations.

Secrets should be changed more often the more they are used. A password-derived key is only as good as the password: if the Appendix A algorithm is used, passwords must be at least 8 characters, and using the same password for authentication and privacy is very poor practice. A user's password or non-localized key MUST NOT be stored on a managed device; the localized key SHALL be stored, if at all.

Sending Reports with noAuthNoPriv may expose an engine to attacks that some consider denial of service. The MIB objects, especially usmUserTable, may be sensitive and should be protected by an access control model such as the View-based Access Control Model.
sections.eli5: A sealed note is still good for a couple of minutes, so a thief could re-send it. Careful devices keep track of what they asked and never trust a password that is easy to guess.

data.title: UsmSecurityParameters
data.code:
UsmSecurityParameters ::=
    SEQUENCE {
        msgAuthoritativeEngineID     OCTET STRING,
        msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots  INTEGER (0..2147483647),
        msgAuthoritativeEngineTime   INTEGER (0..2147483647),
        msgUserName                  OCTET STRING (SIZE(0..32)),
        msgAuthenticationParameters  OCTET STRING,
        msgPrivacyParameters         OCTET STRING
    }
